title: How the God of Israel Was Born
excerpt: From the tablets of Ugarit to the inscriptions of the Sinai: an inquiry into the true origins of monotheism, through biblical layers and archaeological discoveries.
content_html:
In the traditional narrative and in the collective imagination, Judaism is born all at once, in the thunder of Mount Sinai: one God, one Law, a chosen people breaking with the polytheism of neighbouring nations. But the story written in stone and hidden in the folds of the Hebrew Bible's manuscripts (the Tanakh, attested in the Dead Sea Scrolls from Qumran, 3rd century BCE, and in the medieval Hebrew codices of Aleppo and Leningrad) suggests a far more complex history. The original Hebrew text is not a monolith written by a single hand contemporary with the events, but an imposing stratification of independent sources, often openly at odds with one another1.

Modern historical-critical scholarship in particular (following an influential academic reconstruction championed by scholars such as Frank Moore Cross, Mark S. Smith and Thomas Römer) has isolated two major theological and geographical strands: a northern tradition (rooted in the territories of Canaan and tied to the Canaanite culture of Ugarit) and a southern tradition (originating in the Arabian desert and the nomadic tribes). The Judaism we know is the end result of the gradual convergence, smoothing and editorial harmonisation of these two worlds.

1. The North of El: the supreme god, father of the gods

Reading a Bible translation today, the text seems to speak everywhere of a generic "God" or "the Lord". This, however, is a linguistic illusion produced by later confessional versions, which flattened and standardised under abstract categories the distinct proper names and epithets of the oldest Hebrew codices2.

In texts and traditions attributed to the Northern Kingdom (Israel, or Ephraim), attestations of the deity show a clear predominance of titles and epithets referring to El, rendered in precise epithets such as El Shaddai (El of the Mountains, or the Almighty), El Elyon (El the Most High), or in the majestic plural Elohim3. Archaeological excavations conducted since 1929 at the coastal city of Ugarit (in Syria) unearthed a library of cuneiform tablets from the 2nd millennium BCE that describe the Canaanite pantheon in precise detail4.

At Ugarit, El is the supreme, celestial deity: an old, wise and transcendent god, flanked by his consort Asherah (Athirat). El does not intervene directly in human affairs; he delegates the running of the earthly world to his sons, led by the storm god Baal. Under him preside exactly 70 lesser deities, the bn 'il (the "sons of El"), each assigned to protect one of the 70 nations of the then-known world4.

The Hebrew Bible preserves a trace of this divine council in Deuteronomy 32:8-95. In the medieval Masoretic Text, it reads that Elyon divided the nations «according to the number of the sons of Israel». But the Hebrew manuscript from Qumran, 4QDeutj (dating to the 2nd century BCE), and the ancient Greek Septuagint (3rd-2nd century BCE) preserve the older reading: Elyon fixed the borders «according to the number of the sons of Elohim» (benê 'elōhîm), adding that the portion assigned to YHWH was the people of Jacob, suggesting that YHWH was originally conceived not as the supreme god, but as a deity subordinate to El, who had assigned him a single people.

The imprint of this primordial cult is carved into the very name of the people: Isra-El ("El strives" or "May El rule"), not Isra-Yah. Likewise, the names of the patriarchs, prophets and angels tied to the Northern, more archaic tradition end in -el (Samuel, Ezekiel, Gabriel, Michael, Joel, Daniel), testifying to an era when El was the supreme deity of Canaanite territory.

2. The South of YHWH: the god of the desert

The second tradition has its roots in the South. In the Hebrew texts of the South, the god carries the proper, tetragrammatic name YHWH. YHWH is not born in the urban palaces of Canaan, but among the arid highlands and nomadic tribes of Midian, Edom, Seir and the Sinai desert6. Even Egyptian historical sources confirm this: reliefs at the temple of Soleb (dating to Amenhotep III, 14th century BCE) and at Amarah West bear hieroglyphs mentioning the geography of the nomadic Shasu: ta shasu ya-h-wa, meaning "the land of the Shasu of Yhw"7.

The Hebrew Bible itself preserves the memory of this southern geographical rootedness, referring to YHWH with specific territorial epithets tied to the southern desert: YHWH of Teman, YHWH of Seir, or YHWH of Sinai. The god of the South is explicitly described marching from the southern highlands of Edom to aid his devotees in battle (Judges 5:4 and Deuteronomy 33:2)6.

If the Northern tradition used the theophoric ending -el, the Southern tradition and the Kingdom of Judah signed their prophets, kings and priests with the proper name YHWH, ending in -yah or -yahu13. This is the case for prophets and rulers such as Isaiah (Yeshayahu, "YHWH saves"), Jeremiah (Yirmeyahu, "YHWH exalts"), Zechariah (Zekharyahu, "YHWH remembers"), Hezekiah (Hizkiyahu, "YHWH is my strength") and Josiah (Yoshiyahu, "YHWH supports"). Emblematic is the figure of the prophet Elijah, whose Hebrew name Eli-yahu is a synthesis of this encounter, literally meaning «El is YHWH».

The character of YHWH in the archaic texts of the southern tradition is antithetical to that of the transcendent El. YHWH is a concrete, visible, passionate, anthropomorphic god. The text shows him walking in the garden of Eden in the cool of the day (Genesis 3:8), closing the door of Noah's ark with his own hands (Genesis 7:16), or showing Moses his shoulders and back while shielding him in the cleft of the rock (Exodus 33:21-23).

3. The riddle of Moses

The biblical account of the Exodus reflects the historical memory of this encounter between the desert South and Egypt. The very name of Moses is not Hebrew: it derives directly from the Egyptian root mose or msi, simply meaning "born of" or "son" (present in dynastic names such as Thutmose, "son of Thoth", or Ramesses, "son of Ra")8. When Moses flees to Midian after killing an Egyptian overseer beating a Semitic labourer, in the north-western Arabian region identified by Egyptian sources as the cult centre of YHWH, he meets his wife Zipporah. When Zipporah and the other daughters of the priest Reuel/Jethro return home, they describe Moses to their father by saying, explicitly: «An Egyptian delivered us» (Exodus 2:19).

To understand the historical context in which such a figure belongs, one must look at the religious upheavals of Egypt's New Kingdom. In the 14th century BCE, Pharaoh Amenhotep IV (Akhenaten) carried out a violent revolution: he erased the traditional Egyptian pantheon, shut the temples and centralised worship on the single sun-god Aten, with the political aim of sidelining the powerful priesthood of Amun at Thebes9. When Akhenaten died, his young son Tutankhaten was forced by the priests of Amun to restore polytheism, changing his own name to Tutankhamun. After the young ruler's death, the army general Horemheb seized power as pharaoh and decreed a damnatio memoriae against Akhenaten, erasing his name from official cartouches and dismantling the capital at Amarna.

In this climate of religious purges, the thesis of a link between Atenist monotheism and Moses was proposed by Sigmund Freud in his essay Moses and Monotheism (1939). Although Freud's hypothesis of a literally Egyptian, Atenist Moses has remained a minority position among professional Egyptologists, contemporary scholars of cultural memory such as Jan Assmann have explored the trace left in the historical memory of the Near East by the trauma of the Amarna purge108.

An element pointing to shared priestly training between Moses, Aaron and the court of the Nile lies in the episode of the sacred wonders performed before the monarch (Exodus 7:11-12)11. When Aaron throws down his staff and turns it into a serpent, or turns water into blood, Pharaoh's magician-priests (the härtummîm) perform exactly the same secret rituals. Moses and Aaron appear to have mastered the same liturgical and theurgic techniques taught in Egyptian priestly schools. The biblical text does not deny the existence of other gods, nor the power of their cults, but rather asserts the supremacy of the god who guides Moses, whose staff-turned-serpent swallows those of the rival deities.

In Exodus 4:10 Moses excuses himself before the divine calling, claiming to be «slow of speech and slow of tongue» (and in Exodus 6:12 he speaks of «uncircumcised lips»)11. Traditional rabbinic interpretation has read this passage as a physical stutter, but some scholars suggest that Moses, raised as an aristocrat at the Nile court, simply did not master the Semitic dialect spoken by the common people.

Finally, historical research suggests a measured reading of the alleged mass enslavement. In Exodus 1:11, it is said that the Hebrews were put to work building the store-cities of Pithom (Egyptian Per-Atum) and Rameses (Egyptian Pi-Ramesses)8. Archaeological excavations at Tell el-Dab'a and Qantir have confirmed that these cities in the Nile Delta did exist, and were the site of massive royal building projects under the 19th Dynasty8. However, the Semitic populations present in the Delta, tied to the historical memory of the Hyksos, were in all likelihood resident labourers subject to the royal corvée system12. Had two million slaves fled at once, shattering the Egyptian army, the foreign powers of the era (such as the Hittites or the Canaanite city-states in the Amarna letters) would have widely celebrated and documented Egypt's geopolitical collapse. The silence of neighbouring sources indicates there was no catastrophic collapse, but rather a gradual migration back north of groups of Semitic labourers following a priestly elite breaking with Pharaoh's court12.

4. The mystery of the bridegroom of blood

Among the most archaic and unsettling passages in the entire Pentateuch is a very short episode, embedded in Exodus 4:24-2617, which later theology has long tried to soften. Moses has just received the divine order on the mountain to return to Egypt and free the people. But on the journey back, at a resting place in the desert, something incomprehensible happens:

«At a lodging place on the way, YHWH met him and sought to kill him. Then Zipporah took a flint and cut off her son's foreskin and touched Moses's feet with it, and said, "Surely you are a bridegroom of blood to me!" So YHWH let him alone. It was then she said, "A bridegroom of blood," because of the circumcision.»

The text raises a startling question: why does YHWH try to kill the prophet he has just chosen and sent on a mission? And above all, how did Moses's wife know exactly what was happening and which rite would appease YHWH's wrath, if the law of the covenant had not yet been revealed on Sinai?

Zipporah does not hesitate for a second: she grabs a flint stone (not a metal tool, since the oldest ritual tradition of circumcision preserved the use of stone), circumcises her son, and touches Moses's genitals (in the Hebrew euphemism, "feet") with the blood-soaked foreskin, pronouncing the ritual formula Chatan Damim ("bridegroom of blood"). Only then does God relent and withdraw17.

To explain the episode, biblical criticism turns to the Kenite-Midianite Hypothesis (today among the most credited in scholarly debate, though without unanimous consensus). The biblical text explicitly presents Zipporah as the daughter of Reuel/Jethro, the priest of Midian (Exodus 2:16-21). According to the Kenite-Midianite hypothesis, her family had for generations kept the rites of the desert god at Midian, the original geographic cradle of the cult of YHWH. Moses, having grown up at the Egyptian court, had not been circumcised according to the tribal norm of YHWH. Entering the deity's sacred territory without the mark of the covenant, Moses was regarded by YHWH as a profane outsider to be eliminated. Zipporah, knowing the nature of her father's god, performs an immediate apotropaic act: she uses her son's blood to ritually bind Moses to YHWH, making him a "bridegroom of blood" and saving his life.

The Midianite origin and the originally archaic, non-monotheistic character of this cult also emerge clearly from the later encounter between the Israelites and Jethro in the desert (Exodus 18:11), where the Midianite priest exclaims: «Now I know that YHWH is greater than all gods» (mi-kol ha-elohim). In a purely monotheistic context, this statement would make no sense, since one does not call a deity the greatest if the others do not exist. It is the testimony of a monolatrous, henotheistic phase, confirmed by the First Commandment itself (Exodus 20:3: «You shall have no other gods before me»), which forbids the worship of other deities without denying their ontological existence2.

A detail some scholars read as a further clue, though hardly conclusive, follows immediately after, in Exodus 18:12: during the sacrifice that seals the encounter, it is neither Moses nor Aaron who officiates the rite, but Jethro himself, who brings the burnt offering and sacrifices to God, while Aaron and all the elders of Israel simply join the ritual meal "before God" together with Moses's father-in-law. That a Midianite priest presides over the ceremony, rather than the two Hebrew leaders fresh out of Egypt, has sometimes been read as a possible sign that Jethro was not merely joining someone else's cult, but already held a recognised priestly role toward YHWH; this remains an inference, though, not a settled fact.

5. The Levites: the birth of a priestly caste

The Egyptian legacy and ideological fanaticism converged into a single tribe: the Levites. Among the twelve tribes of Israel, the priestly tribe of the Levites is the only one to preserve several names of credited Egyptian etymology, such as Moses (from Egyptian Msi, "born of"), Phinehas (from Egyptian Pa-nehesi, "the Nubian"), Hophni (from Egyptian Hfnw, "tadpole") and Pashhur (from Egyptian p3 sri n ḥr or pss-ḥr, "son of Horus" or "portion of Horus").

The key episode of rigid priestly fanaticism takes place during the march through the desert: the story of the Golden Calf (Exodus 32)13. Faced with the masses' return to the syncretic cults they had betrayed, Moses gathers the Levites and orders a systematic slaughter: three thousand men (including brothers, friends and neighbours) are massacred by the priests to impose, with blood, the exclusive monotheistic cult of YHWH (Exodus 32:26-28).

Beyond the ideological violence, the Levites brought into the desert a sophisticated ritual culture unknown to the nomads of Sinai, modelled almost entirely on the liturgy of the Nile temples14. Levitical priests were required to wear only pure linen garments (shesh, from the Egyptian term šs), with wool strictly forbidden (Leviticus 6:3)14. This is a telling prescription: wool was the natural fibre produced daily by the desert's nomadic populations through sheep and goat herding, while linen required sowing, cultivation and irrigation on fertile farmland, a resource typical of the Nile valley and entirely impossible to produce in the desert. Mandating linen and excluding wool means the priestly norm did not originate among the Bedouin of Sinai, but was imported directly from the prescriptive sacred dress of the Egyptian priestly caste. Likewise, the daily purification rituals with water, the full-body shaving required of the Levites (Numbers 8:7) and the prohibition on contact with corpses mirror the rules of the Karnak sanctuaries. Finally, the structure of the Tabernacle and the proportions of the Ark of the Covenant are identical to the military encampment of Ramesses II at the Battle of Kadesh and to the gilded wooden shrines found in Tutankhamun's tomb15. Taken individually, these elements do not amount to proof. Taken together, they have been interpreted by some scholars as evidence of a significant Egyptian influence on the formation of the Levitical tradition.

6. The merger of the two traditions

Once settled in the land of Canaan, the Levites consolidated their position. Being the only tribe not to have inherited a geographic territory (Numbers 18:20-24) (perhaps precisely because they arrived later from Egypt, when the other tribes had already settled the area), they secured their economic livelihood by collecting tithes from all the other eleven tribes for cultic services. In the following centuries, this position allowed the priestly caste to vastly expand its political influence.

To unify the people and prevent theological schisms between the cults of the North and the South, the priests carried out a colossal exegetical rewriting. The figures of El and YHWH were unified into a single God. The 70 sons of El became the 70 members of Jacob's family who went down into Egypt (Genesis 46:27), while the figure of Asherah, El's heavenly consort, was systematically erased from the official texts.

The decisive turn toward strict, exclusive monotheism was imposed in 622 BCE under the reign of Josiah in Jerusalem. The text of 2 Kings 22:8 recounts that the high priest Hilkiah, himself a member of the Levitical priestly caste, declared he had "accidentally rediscovered" in the basements of the Temple the "book of the Law" (identified by historians with the core of Deuteronomy)1. In imposing this text, the Levitical priests attempted precisely the same authoritarian operation attempted centuries earlier at Amarna for Aten: the imperial shutdown of all local shrines, the systematic destruction of altars and sacred poles (the Asherim) standing beside them (Deuteronomy 16:21 and 2 Kings 23:6), the elimination of traditional cults, and the absolute centralisation of all liturgical and economic power in Jerusalem.

7. The great harmonisation

Perhaps the memory of the bloody purges and revolts that had erupted centuries earlier in Egypt after Akhenaten's fall was still alive in cultural memory, or perhaps political pragmatism prevailed: whatever the case, the priestly caste and the post-exilic editors carried out an immense work of "cutting, stitching and merging". Instead of abruptly erasing the competing narratives, they wove them into a single, apparently harmonious garment, smoothing over the points of friction, but leaving on the biblical text indelible imprints, logical short-circuits and blatant mythological borrowings.

The editor's admission: YHWH concedes he revealed himself as El

The testimony of this complex work of editorial synthesis is contained in Exodus 6:2-31. Here the priestly redaction inserts a genuine statement of synthesis for the benefit of readers disoriented by the plurality of names in the stories of Genesis:

«God spoke to Moses and said to him, "I am YHWH. I appeared to Abraham, to Isaac and to Jacob as El Shaddai, but by my name YHWH I did not make myself known to them."»

This passage reveals the redactors' strategy: knowing that in the archaic Northern texts and the patriarchal stories God was invoked exclusively by the Canaanite names El or El Shaddai, the redactors insert after the fact a theological explanation that forcibly unifies the cults. In effect, they make YHWH say: "It was me all along, only I hadn't told you my true name yet." It is the decisive move by which the 70 sons of El are reread and reabsorbed into the new monotheistic framework.

The birth story of Moses: a hypothesis of editorial addition

A second intervention concerns the figure of the founder. Many features of the biblical text and several historical clues suggest that Moses may originally have been a figure of Egyptian extraction: he bore a proper Egyptian name (Mose/Msi), spoke the language of the court, making the interpreter Aaron necessary (Exodus 4:10), was described by Jethro's daughters as «an Egyptian» (Exodus 2:19), and mastered the very same theurgic rituals as Pharaoh's priests (Exodus 7:11-12).

According to a widely held hypothesis in historical-critical scholarship, the infancy narrative in Exodus 2:1-10 may represent a later editorial addition. Its main function would not have been merely to give the leader a dramatic origin story, but above all to furnish Moses with a biological Hebrew genealogy, having him born into a family of the tribe of Levi and reinterpreting his Egyptian name through a popular Hebrew etymology (Mosheh, understood as "drawn out of the water")8.

To build this infancy narrative, the scribes applied to Moses the most famous kingship narrative of the ancient Near East: the Legend of Sargon of Akkad (23rd century BCE), inscribed on Neo-Assyrian tablets well known to the Jews in Babylon12. In the Mesopotamian tale, a priestess mother conceives Sargon in secret, places him in a reed basket sealed with bitumen and entrusts him to the waters of the river, where he is rescued and rises to the throne. The scribes of Exodus reused this pattern: Moses's mother hides him for three months, places him in a papyrus basket (tebah) sealed with pitch, and sets him adrift on the Nile.

This narrative modelled on Sargon is the Mesopotamian instance of a much broader shared literary topos: the motif of the "predestined child" saved from the waters and raised in ignorance of his true origins to fulfil a hero's mission. It is a narrative pattern found across countless ancient and modern cultures: from Oedipus to Romulus and Remus, to the nativity accounts of Jesus with the flight into Egypt to escape Herod's slaughter of the innocents, and even in contemporary pop-culture myths such as the story of Superman (sent off in a space cradle as a newborn to escape the destruction of his civilisation, and then raised by an earthly family).

The grafting of this childhood narrative also produces conspicuous short-circuits and anachronisms. The Bible calls Moses's mother Jochebed (Yocheved, Exodus 6:20), a name meaning «YHWH is glory». But when Moses is born, the name YHWH had not yet been revealed to anyone, since, as noted, the revelation of the divine name would only occur much later, when Moses is already an adult on Mount Sinai. This detail may reflect an inconsistency, or a later layer of redaction. Likewise, the story betrays its naively aetiological nature: if Pharaoh had decreed the killing of all newborn Hebrew boys, it is unclear how the elder brother Aaron (only three years older than Moses) (Exodus 7:7) was born and raised freely without the family having had to hide him. But above all, the narrative turn in which the sister Miriam, a young Semitic girl, casually approaches Pharaoh's daughter on the riverbank just as she is fishing the basket out of the water, and promptly offers to hire, as a paid wet-nurse, the very biological mother who had just set the infant adrift, appears entirely naive.

Historical conclusion

The reconstruction offered by modern biblical scholarship and archaeology shows how the birth of Jewish monotheism was the outcome of a long and fascinating historical-cultural process. Judaism did not arise suddenly, nor in isolation from the context of the ancient Near East, but developed through the convergence and stratification of distinct traditions: the transcendent solemnity of the Canaanite El, the energy of the desert god YHWH, the liturgical influences born of contact with Egypt, and the centralising processes promoted by the rulers of Judah in Jerusalem.

This trajectory shows that the sacred texts of antiquity are not immutable monoliths written once and for all, but an extraordinary, plural library that preserves the traces of the eras, social tensions and cultural contexts in which they were born and transformed over the centuries.

A personal reflection

Beyond the historical-critical reconstruction of ancient Near Eastern cults, the dynamic of reworking texts held to be sacred has continued uninterrupted into later religious traditions. A well-known example in Catholic Christianity is the catechetical reorganisation of the Ten Commandments, in which the original biblical prohibition on making carved images of God found in Exodus 20:4 was folded into the First Commandment, and the tenth precept was split into two parts ("do not covet your neighbour's wife" and "do not covet your neighbour's goods") to preserve the count of ten, adapting the ancient biblical structure to the pedagogical and theological needs of the catechism.

Ancient and contemporary history also demonstrates a recurring pattern whenever religious power takes precedence over political power in imposing its own theocracy: from the dark centuries of European history (marked by the devastation of the Crusades, the pyres of the Inquisition and the persecutions of the witch hunts) to events in the contemporary world, such as the turning point of the 1979 Islamic Revolution in Iran, when a rapidly secularising country was transformed into a rigid clerical theocracy stripped of individual freedoms.

Finally, a note on sources. For the sake of practicality, and to allow anyone free and immediate access on the web, in the bibliographic notes I chose to cite open encyclopedic entries directly (such as Wikipedia) or consultable text databases (such as BibleGateway). For those who wish to go deeper on the scholarly level, the historical-critical, philological and epigraphic thread of this inquiry draws on the work of the field's leading contemporary authors and scholars, whom I invite readers to consult: Mark S. Smith, Thomas Römer, John Day, Israel Finkelstein, William G. Dever, Francesca Stavrakopoulou, Frank Moore Cross, Karel van der Toorn and Jan Assmann.

Recognising the historical, human and plural dimension of the Hebrew Bible does not diminish its fascination, but restores it to its most authentic and living nature: that of a grand collective memory that keeps questioning us about our past.

The Hebrew Bible itself preserves the memory of this southern geographical rootedness, referring to YHWH with specific territorial epithets tied to the southern desert: YHWH of Teman, YHWH of Seir, or YHWH of Sinai. The god of the South is explicitly described marching from the southern highlands of Edom to aid his devotees in battle (Judges 5:4 and Deuteronomy 33:2)6. If the Northern tradition used the theophoric ending -el, the Southern tradition and the Kingdom of Judah signed their prophets, kings and priests with the proper name YHWH, ending in -yah or -yahu13. This is the case for prophets and rulers such as Isaiah (Yeshayahu, "YHWH saves"), Jeremiah (Yirmeyahu, "YHWH exalts"), Zechariah (Zekharyahu, "YHWH remembers"), Hezekiah (Hizkiyahu, "YHWH is my strength") and Josiah (Yoshiyahu, "YHWH supports"). Emblematic is the figure of the prophet Elijah, whose Hebrew name Eli-yahu is a synthesis of this encounter, literally meaning «El is YHWH». The character of YHWH in the archaic texts of the southern tradition is antithetical to that of the transcendent El. YHWH is a concrete, visible, passionate, anthropomorphic god. The text shows him walking in the garden of Eden in the cool of the day (Genesis 3:8), closing the door of Noah's ark with his own hands (Genesis 7:16), or showing Moses his shoulders and back while shielding him in the cleft of the rock (Exodus 33:21-23). 3. The riddle of Moses The biblical account of the Exodus reflects the historical memory of this encounter between the desert South and Egypt. The very name of Moses is not Hebrew: it derives directly from the Egyptian root mose or msi, simply meaning "born of" or "son" (present in dynastic names such as Thutmose, "son of Thoth", or Ramesses, "son of Ra")8. When Moses flees to Midian after killing an Egyptian overseer beating a Semitic labourer, in the north-western Arabian region identified by Egyptian sources as the cult centre of YHWH, he meets his wife Zipporah. When Zipporah and the other daughters of the priest Reuel/Jethro return home, they describe Moses to their father by saying, explicitly: «An Egyptian delivered us» (Exodus 2:19). To understand the historical context in which such a figure belongs, one must look at the religious upheavals of Egypt's New Kingdom. In the 14th century BCE, Pharaoh Amenhotep IV (Akhenaten) carried out a violent revolution: he erased the traditional Egyptian pantheon, shut the temples and centralised worship on the single sun-god Aten, with the political aim of sidelining the powerful priesthood of Amun at Thebes9. When Akhenaten died, his young son Tutankhaten was forced by the priests of Amun to restore polytheism, changing his own name to Tutankhamun. After the young ruler's death, the army general Horemheb seized power as pharaoh and decreed a damnatio memoriae against Akhenaten, erasing his name from official cartouches and dismantling the capital at Amarna. In this climate of religious purges, the thesis of a link between Atenist monotheism and Moses was proposed by Sigmund Freud in his essay Moses and Monotheism (1939). Although Freud's hypothesis of a literally Egyptian, Atenist Moses has remained a minority position among professional Egyptologists, contemporary scholars of cultural memory such as Jan Assmann have explored the trace left in the historical memory of the Near East by the trauma of the Amarna purge108. An element pointing to shared priestly training between Moses, Aaron and the court of the Nile lies in the episode of the sacred wonders performed before the monarch (Exodus 7:11-12)11. When Aaron throws down his staff and turns it into a serpent, or turns water into blood, Pharaoh's magician-priests (the härtummîm) perform exactly the same secret rituals. Moses and Aaron appear to have mastered the same liturgical and theurgic techniques taught in Egyptian priestly schools. The biblical text does not deny the existence of other gods, nor the power of their cults, but rather asserts the supremacy of the god who guides Moses, whose staff-turned-serpent swallows those of the rival deities. In Exodus 4:10 Moses excuses himself before the divine calling, claiming to be «slow of speech and slow of tongue» (and in Exodus 6:12 he speaks of «uncircumcised lips»)11. Traditional rabbinic interpretation has read this passage as a physical stutter, but some scholars suggest that Moses, raised as an aristocrat at the Nile court, simply did not master the Semitic dialect spoken by the common people. Finally, historical research suggests a measured reading of the alleged mass enslavement. In Exodus 1:11, it is said that the Hebrews were put to work building the store-cities of Pithom (Egyptian Per-Atum) and Rameses (Egyptian Pi-Ramesses)8. Archaeological excavations at Tell el-Dab'a and Qantir have confirmed that these cities in the Nile Delta did exist, and were the site of massive royal building projects under the 19th Dynasty8. However, the Semitic populations present in the Delta, tied to the historical memory of the Hyksos, were in all likelihood resident labourers subject to the royal corvée system12. Had two million slaves fled at once, shattering the Egyptian army, the foreign powers of the era (such as the Hittites or the Canaanite city-states in the Amarna letters) would have widely celebrated and documented Egypt's geopolitical collapse. The silence of neighbouring sources indicates there was no catastrophic collapse, but rather a gradual migration back north of groups of Semitic labourers following a priestly elite breaking with Pharaoh's court12. 4. The mystery of the bridegroom of blood Among the most archaic and unsettling passages in the entire Pentateuch is a very short episode, embedded in Exodus 4:24-2617, which later theology has long tried to soften. Moses has just received the divine order on the mountain to return to Egypt and free the people. But on the journey back, at a resting place in the desert, something incomprehensible happens: «At a lodging place on the way, YHWH met him and sought to kill him. Then Zipporah took a flint and cut off her son's foreskin and touched Moses's feet with it, and said, "Surely you are a bridegroom of blood to me!" So YHWH let him alone. It was then she said, "A bridegroom of blood," because of the circumcision.» The text raises a startling question: why does YHWH try to kill the prophet he has just chosen and sent on a mission? And above all, how did Moses's wife know exactly what was happening and which rite would appease YHWH's wrath, if the law of the covenant had not yet been revealed on Sinai? Zipporah does not hesitate for a second: she grabs a flint stone (not a metal tool, since the oldest ritual tradition of circumcision preserved the use of stone), circumcises her son, and touches Moses's genitals (in the Hebrew euphemism, "feet") with the blood-soaked foreskin, pronouncing the ritual formula Chatan Damim ("bridegroom of blood"). Only then does God relent and withdraw17. To explain the episode, biblical criticism turns to the Kenite-Midianite Hypothesis (today among the most credited in scholarly debate, though without unanimous consensus). The biblical text explicitly presents Zipporah as the daughter of Reuel/Jethro, the priest of Midian (Exodus 2:16-21). According to the Kenite-Midianite hypothesis, her family had for generations kept the rites of the desert god at Midian, the original geographic cradle of the cult of YHWH. Moses, having grown up at the Egyptian court, had not been circumcised according to the tribal norm of YHWH. Entering the deity's sacred territory without the mark of the covenant, Moses was regarded by YHWH as a profane outsider to be eliminated. Zipporah, knowing the nature of her father's god, performs an immediate apotropaic act: she uses her son's blood to ritually bind Moses to YHWH, making him a "bridegroom of blood" and saving his life. The Midianite origin and the originally archaic, non-monotheistic character of this cult also emerge clearly from the later encounter between the Israelites and Jethro in the desert (Exodus 18:11), where the Midianite priest exclaims: «Now I know that YHWH is greater than all gods» (mi-kol ha-elohim). In a purely monotheistic context, this statement would make no sense, since one does not call a deity the greatest if the others do not exist. It is the testimony of a monolatrous, henotheistic phase, confirmed by the First Commandment itself (Exodus 20:3: «You shall have no other gods before me»), which forbids the worship of other deities without denying their ontological existence2. A detail some scholars read as a further clue, though hardly conclusive, follows immediately after, in Exodus 18:12: during the sacrifice that seals the encounter, it is neither Moses nor Aaron who officiates the rite, but Jethro himself, who brings the burnt offering and sacrifices to God, while Aaron and all the elders of Israel simply join the ritual meal "before God" together with Moses's father-in-law. That a Midianite priest presides over the ceremony, rather than the two Hebrew leaders fresh out of Egypt, has sometimes been read as a possible sign that Jethro was not merely joining someone else's cult, but already held a recognised priestly role toward YHWH; this remains an inference, though, not a settled fact. 5. The Levites: the birth of a priestly caste The Egyptian legacy and ideological fanaticism converged into a single tribe: the Levites. Among the twelve tribes of Israel, the priestly tribe of the Levites is the only one to preserve several names of credited Egyptian etymology, such as Moses (from Egyptian Msi, "born of"), Phinehas (from Egyptian Pa-nehesi, "the Nubian"), Hophni (from Egyptian Hfnw, "tadpole") and Pashhur (from Egyptian p3 sri n ḥr or pss-ḥr, "son of Horus" or "portion of Horus"). The key episode of rigid priestly fanaticism takes place during the march through the desert: the story of the Golden Calf (Exodus 32)13. Faced with the masses' return to the syncretic cults they had betrayed, Moses gathers the Levites and orders a systematic slaughter: three thousand men (including brothers, friends and neighbours) are massacred by the priests to impose, with blood, the exclusive monotheistic cult of YHWH (Exodus 32:26-28). Beyond the ideological violence, the Levites brought into the desert a sophisticated ritual culture unknown to the nomads of Sinai, modelled almost entirely on the liturgy of the Nile temples14. Levitical priests were required to wear only pure linen garments (shesh, from the Egyptian term šs), with wool strictly forbidden (Leviticus 6:3)14. This is a telling prescription: wool was the natural fibre produced daily by the desert's nomadic populations through sheep and goat herding, while linen required sowing, cultivation and irrigation on fertile farmland, a resource typical of the Nile valley and entirely impossible to produce in the desert. Mandating linen and excluding wool means the priestly norm did not originate among the Bedouin of Sinai, but was imported directly from the prescriptive sacred dress of the Egyptian priestly caste. Likewise, the daily purification rituals with water, the full-body shaving required of the Levites (Numbers 8:7) and the prohibition on contact with corpses mirror the rules of the Karnak sanctuaries. Finally, the structure of the Tabernacle and the proportions of the Ark of the Covenant are identical to the military encampment of Ramesses II at the Battle of Kadesh and to the gilded wooden shrines found in Tutankhamun's tomb15. Taken individually, these elements do not amount to proof. Taken together, they have been interpreted by some scholars as evidence of a significant Egyptian influence on the formation of the Levitical tradition. 6. The merger of the two traditions Once settled in the land of Canaan, the Levites consolidated their position. Being the only tribe not to have inherited a geographic territory (Numbers 18:20-24) (perhaps precisely because they arrived later from Egypt, when the other tribes had already settled the area), they secured their economic livelihood by collecting tithes from all the other eleven tribes for cultic services. In the following centuries, this position allowed the priestly caste to vastly expand its political influence. To unify the people and prevent theological schisms between the cults of the North and the South, the priests carried out a colossal exegetical rewriting. The figures of El and YHWH were unified into a single God. The 70 sons of El became the 70 members of Jacob's family who went down into Egypt (Genesis 46:27), while the figure of Asherah, El's heavenly consort, was systematically erased from the official texts. The decisive turn toward strict, exclusive monotheism was imposed in 622 BCE under the reign of Josiah in Jerusalem. The text of 2 Kings 22:8 recounts that the high priest Hilkiah, himself a member of the Levitical priestly caste, declared he had "accidentally rediscovered" in the basements of the Temple the "book of the Law" (identified by historians with the core of Deuteronomy)1. In imposing this text, the Levitical priests attempted precisely the same authoritarian operation attempted centuries earlier at Amarna for Aten: the imperial shutdown of all local shrines, the systematic destruction of altars and sacred poles (the Asherim) standing beside them (Deuteronomy 16:21 and 2 Kings 23:6), the elimination of traditional cults, and the absolute centralisation of all liturgical and economic power in Jerusalem. 7. The great harmonisation Perhaps the memory of the bloody purges and revolts that had erupted centuries earlier in Egypt after Akhenaten's fall was still alive in cultural memory, or perhaps political pragmatism prevailed: whatever the case, the priestly caste and the post-exilic editors carried out an immense work of "cutting, stitching and merging". Instead of abruptly erasing the competing narratives, they wove them into a single, apparently harmonious garment, smoothing over the points of friction, but leaving on the biblical text indelible imprints, logical short-circuits and blatant mythological borrowings. The editor's admission: YHWH concedes he revealed himself as El The testimony of this complex work of editorial synthesis is contained in Exodus 6:2-31. Here the priestly redaction inserts a genuine statement of synthesis for the benefit of readers disoriented by the plurality of names in the stories of Genesis: «God spoke to Moses and said to him, "I am YHWH. I appeared to Abraham, to Isaac and to Jacob as El Shaddai, but by my name YHWH I did not make myself known to them."» This passage reveals the redactors' strategy: knowing that in the archaic Northern texts and the patriarchal stories God was invoked exclusively by the Canaanite names El or El Shaddai, the redactors insert after the fact a theological explanation that forcibly unifies the cults. In effect, they make YHWH say: "It was me all along, only I hadn't told you my true name yet." It is the decisive move by which the 70 sons of El are reread and reabsorbed into the new monotheistic framework. The birth story of Moses: a hypothesis of editorial addition A second intervention concerns the figure of the founder. Many features of the biblical text and several historical clues suggest that Moses may originally have been a figure of Egyptian extraction: he bore a proper Egyptian name (Mose/Msi), spoke the language of the court, making the interpreter Aaron necessary (Exodus 4:10), was described by Jethro's daughters as «an Egyptian» (Exodus 2:19), and mastered the very same theurgic rituals as Pharaoh's priests (Exodus 7:11-12). According to a widely held hypothesis in historical-critical scholarship, the infancy narrative in Exodus 2:1-10 may represent a later editorial addition. Its main function would not have been merely to give the leader a dramatic origin story, but above all to furnish Moses with a biological Hebrew genealogy, having him born into a family of the tribe of Levi and reinterpreting his Egyptian name through a popular Hebrew etymology (Mosheh, understood as "drawn out of the water")8. To build this infancy narrative, the scribes applied to Moses the most famous kingship narrative of the ancient Near East: the Legend of Sargon of Akkad (23rd century BCE), inscribed on Neo-Assyrian tablets well known to the Jews in Babylon12. In the Mesopotamian tale, a priestess mother conceives Sargon in secret, places him in a reed basket sealed with bitumen and entrusts him to the waters of the river, where he is rescued and rises to the throne. The scribes of Exodus reused this pattern: Moses's mother hides him for three months, places him in a papyrus basket (tebah) sealed with pitch, and sets him adrift on the Nile. This narrative modelled on Sargon is the Mesopotamian instance of a much broader shared literary topos: the motif of the "predestined child" saved from the waters and raised in ignorance of his true origins to fulfil a hero's mission. It is a narrative pattern found across countless ancient and modern cultures: from Oedipus to Romulus and Remus, to the nativity accounts of Jesus with the flight into Egypt to escape Herod's slaughter of the innocents, and even in contemporary pop-culture myths such as the story of Superman (sent off in a space cradle as a newborn to escape the destruction of his civilisation, and then raised by an earthly family). The grafting of this childhood narrative also produces conspicuous short-circuits and anachronisms. The Bible calls Moses's mother Jochebed (Yocheved, Exodus 6:20), a name meaning «YHWH is glory». But when Moses is born, the name YHWH had not yet been revealed to anyone, since, as noted, the revelation of the divine name would only occur much later, when Moses is already an adult on Mount Sinai. This detail may reflect an inconsistency, or a later layer of redaction. Likewise, the story betrays its naively aetiological nature: if Pharaoh had decreed the killing of all newborn Hebrew boys, it is unclear how the elder brother Aaron (only three years older than Moses) (Exodus 7:7) was born and raised freely without the family having had to hide him. But above all, the narrative turn in which the sister Miriam, a young Semitic girl, casually approaches Pharaoh's daughter on the riverbank just as she is fishing the basket out of the water, and promptly offers to hire, as a paid wet-nurse, the very biological mother who had just set the infant adrift, appears entirely naive. Historical conclusion The reconstruction offered by modern biblical scholarship and archaeology shows how the birth of Jewish monotheism was the outcome of a long and fascinating historical-cultural process. Judaism did not arise suddenly, nor in isolation from the context of the ancient Near East, but developed through the convergence and stratification of distinct traditions: the transcendent solemnity of the Canaanite El, the energy of the desert god YHWH, the liturgical influences born of contact with Egypt, and the centralising processes promoted by the rulers of Judah in Jerusalem. This trajectory shows that the sacred texts of antiquity are not immutable monoliths written once and for all, but an extraordinary, plural library that preserves the traces of the eras, social tensions and cultural contexts in which they were born and transformed over the centuries. A personal reflection Beyond the historical-critical reconstruction of ancient Near Eastern cults, the dynamic of reworking texts held to be sacred has continued uninterrupted into later religious traditions. A well-known example in Catholic Christianity is the catechetical reorganisation of the Ten Commandments, in which the original biblical prohibition on making carved images of God found in Exodus 20:4 was folded into the First Commandment, and the tenth precept was split into two parts ("do not covet your neighbour's wife" and "do not covet your neighbour's goods") to preserve the count of ten, adapting the ancient biblical structure to the pedagogical and theological needs of the catechism. Ancient and contemporary history also demonstrates a recurring pattern whenever religious power takes precedence over political power in imposing its own theocracy: from the dark centuries of European history (marked by the devastation of the Crusades, the pyres of the Inquisition and the persecutions of the witch hunts) to events in the contemporary world, such as the turning point of the 1979 Islamic Revolution in Iran, when a rapidly secularising country was transformed into a rigid clerical theocracy stripped of individual freedoms. Finally, a note on sources. For the sake of practicality, and to allow anyone free and immediate access on the web, in the bibliographic notes I chose to cite open encyclopedic entries directly (such as Wikipedia) or consultable text databases (such as BibleGateway). For those who wish to go deeper on the scholarly level, the historical-critical, philological and epigraphic thread of this inquiry draws on the work of the field's leading contemporary authors and scholars, whom I invite readers to consult: Mark S. Smith, Thomas Römer, John Day, Israel Finkelstein, William G. Dever, Francesca Stavrakopoulou, Frank Moore Cross, Karel van der Toorn and Jan Assmann. Recognising the historical, human and plural dimension of the Hebrew Bible does not diminish its fascination, but restores it to its most authentic and living nature: that of a grand collective memory that keeps questioning us about our past. blocks.html_en: In the traditional narrative and in the collective imagination, Judaism is born all at once, in the thunder of Mount Sinai: one God, one Law, a chosen people breaking with the polytheism of neighbouring nations. But the story written in stone and hidden in the folds of the Hebrew Bible's manuscripts (the Tanakh, attested in the Dead Sea Scrolls from Qumran, 3rd century BCE, and in the medieval Hebrew codices of Aleppo and Leningrad) suggests a far more complex history. The original Hebrew text is not a monolith written by a single hand contemporary with the events, but an imposing stratification of independent sources, often openly at odds with one another1.

blocks.html_en: At Ugarit, El is the supreme, celestial deity: an old, wise and transcendent god, flanked by his consort Asherah (Athirat). El does not intervene directly in human affairs; he delegates the running of the earthly world to his sons, led by the storm god Baal. Under him preside exactly 70 lesser deities, the bn 'il (the "sons of El"), each assigned to protect one of the 70 nations of the then-known world4.

sentences.en: At Ugarit, El is the supreme, celestial deity: an old, wise and transcendent god, flanked by his consort Asherah (Athirat).
sentences.zh: 在乌加里特，埃尔是至高无上的天神：一位古老、智慧和超然的神，两侧是他的配偶亚舍拉（Athirat）。

sentences.en: El does not intervene directly in human affairs; he delegates the running of the earthly world to his sons, led by the storm god Baal.
sentences.zh: 艾尔不直接干预人类事务；他将尘世的管理权委托给了由风暴之神巴力领导的儿子们。

sentences.en: Under him preside exactly 70 lesser deities, the bn 'il (the "sons of El"), each assigned to protect one of the 70 nations of the then-known world4.
sentences.zh: 在他的领导下，正好有 70 个较小的神，即 bn'il（“埃尔之子”），每个神都被指派保护当时已知世界 70 个国家中的一个。

blocks.html_en: The Hebrew Bible preserves a trace of this divine council in Deuteronomy 32:8-95. In the medieval Masoretic Text, it reads that Elyon divided the nations «according to the number of the sons of Israel». But the Hebrew manuscript from Qumran, 4QDeutj (dating to the 2nd century BCE), and the ancient Greek Septuagint (3rd-2nd century BCE) preserve the older reading: Elyon fixed the borders «according to the number of the sons of Elohim» (benê 'elōhîm), adding that the portion assigned to YHWH was the people of Jacob, suggesting that YHWH was originally conceived not as the supreme god, but as a deity subordinate to El, who had assigned him a single people.

sentences.en: The Hebrew Bible preserves a trace of this divine council in Deuteronomy 32:8-95.
sentences.zh: 希伯来圣经在申命记 32:8-95 中保留了这一神圣会议的痕迹。

sentences.en: In the medieval Masoretic Text, it reads that Elyon divided the nations «according to the number of the sons of Israel».
sentences.zh: 在中世纪的马所拉文本中，埃利昂“根据以色列儿子的数量”划分了国家。

sentences.en: But the Hebrew manuscript from Qumran, 4QDeutj (dating to the 2nd century BCE), and the ancient Greek Septuagint (3rd-2nd century BCE) preserve the older reading: Elyon fixed the borders «according to the number of the sons of Elohim» (benê 'elōhîm), adding that the portion assigned to YHWH was the people of Jacob, suggesting that YHWH was originally conceived not as the supreme god, but as a deity subordinate to El, who had assigned him a single people.
sentences.zh: 但库姆兰的希伯来语手稿 4QDeutj（可追溯到公元前 2 世纪）和古希腊语《七十士译本》（公元前 3-2 世纪）保留了较旧的解读：Elyon“根据埃洛希姆儿子的数量”（benê 'elōhîm）确定了边界，并补充说分配给耶和华的部分是雅各的子民，这表明耶和华最初并不被视为至高无上的神，但作为埃尔的下属神，埃尔给他分配了一个民族。

blocks.html_en: The imprint of this primordial cult is carved into the very name of the people: Isra-El ("El strives" or "May El rule"), not Isra-Yah. Likewise, the names of the patriarchs, prophets and angels tied to the Northern, more archaic tradition end in -el (Samuel, Ezekiel, Gabriel, Michael, Joel, Daniel), testifying to an era when El was the supreme deity of Canaanite territory.

sentences.en: The imprint of this primordial cult is carved into the very name of the people: Isra-El ("El strives" or "May El rule"), not Isra-Yah.
sentences.zh: 这种原始崇拜的印记被刻在了人们的名字中：Isra-El（“El 奋斗”或“May El 统治”），而不是 Isra-Yah。

blocks.html_en: 2. The South of YHWH: the god of the desert

sentences.en: The South of YHWH: the god of the desert
sentences.zh: 耶和华的南方：沙漠之神

blocks.html_en: The second tradition has its roots in the South. In the Hebrew texts of the South, the god carries the proper, tetragrammatic name YHWH. YHWH is not born in the urban palaces of Canaan, but among the arid highlands and nomadic tribes of Midian, Edom, Seir and the Sinai desert6. Even Egyptian historical sources confirm this: reliefs at the temple of Soleb (dating to Amenhotep III, 14th century BCE) and at Amarah West bear hieroglyphs mentioning the geography of the nomadic Shasu: ta shasu ya-h-wa, meaning "the land of the Shasu of Yhw"7.

sentences.en: The second tradition has its roots in the South.
sentences.zh: 第二个传统起源于南方。

sentences.en: In the Hebrew texts of the South, the god carries the proper, tetragrammatic name YHWH.
sentences.zh: 在南方的希伯来语文本中，这位神具有正确的四语法名称 YHWH。

sentences.en: YHWH is not born in the urban palaces of Canaan, but among the arid highlands and nomadic tribes of Midian, Edom, Seir and the Sinai desert6.
sentences.zh: 耶和华并不是诞生在迦南的城市宫殿中，而是诞生在米甸、以东、西珥和西奈沙漠的干旱高地和游牧部落中。

sentences.en: Even Egyptian historical sources confirm this: reliefs at the temple of Soleb (dating to Amenhotep III, 14th century BCE) and at Amarah West bear hieroglyphs mentioning the geography of the nomadic Shasu: ta shasu ya-h-wa, meaning "the land of the Shasu of Yhw"7.
sentences.zh: 甚至埃及的历史资料也证实了这一点：索莱布神庙（可追溯到公元前 14 世纪阿蒙霍特普三世）和阿玛拉西的浮雕上都有象形文字，提到了游牧沙苏的地理：ta shasu ya-h-wa，意思是“耶和华沙苏的土地”7。

blocks.html_en: The Hebrew Bible itself preserves the memory of this southern geographical rootedness, referring to YHWH with specific territorial epithets tied to the southern desert: YHWH of Teman, YHWH of Seir, or YHWH of Sinai. The god of the South is explicitly described marching from the southern highlands of Edom to aid his devotees in battle (Judges 5:4 and Deuteronomy 33:2)6.

sentences.en: The Hebrew Bible itself preserves the memory of this southern geographical rootedness, referring to YHWH with specific territorial epithets tied to the southern desert: YHWH of Teman, YHWH of Seir, or YHWH of Sinai.
sentences.zh: 希伯来圣经本身保留了这种南部地理根源的记忆，用与南部沙漠相关的特定领土绰号来指代耶和华：提曼的耶和华、西珥的耶和华或西奈的耶和华。

sentences.en: The god of the South is explicitly described marching from the southern highlands of Edom to aid his devotees in battle (Judges 5:4 and Deuteronomy 33:2)6.
sentences.zh: 南方之神被明确描述为从以东南部高地出发，在战斗中帮助他的信徒（士师记 5:4 和申命记 33:2）6。

blocks.html_en: If the Northern tradition used the theophoric ending -el, the Southern tradition and the Kingdom of Judah signed their prophets, kings and priests with the proper name YHWH, ending in -yah or -yahu13. This is the case for prophets and rulers such as Isaiah (Yeshayahu, "YHWH saves"), Jeremiah (Yirmeyahu, "YHWH exalts"), Zechariah (Zekharyahu, "YHWH remembers"), Hezekiah (Hizkiyahu, "YHWH is my strength") and Josiah (Yoshiyahu, "YHWH supports"). Emblematic is the figure of the prophet Elijah, whose Hebrew name Eli-yahu is a synthesis of this encounter, literally meaning «El is YHWH».

sentences.en: If the Northern tradition used the theophoric ending -el, the Southern tradition and the Kingdom of Judah signed their prophets, kings and priests with the proper name YHWH, ending in -yah or -yahu13.
sentences.zh: 如果北方传统使用神喻结尾 -el，那么南方传统和犹大王国则用专有名称 YHWH 来签署他们的先知、国王和祭司，并以 -yah 或 -yahu13 结尾。

sentences.en: This is the case for prophets and rulers such as Isaiah (Yeshayahu, "YHWH saves"), Jeremiah (Yirmeyahu, "YHWH exalts"), Zechariah (Zekharyahu, "YHWH remembers"), Hezekiah (Hizkiyahu, "YHWH is my strength") and Josiah (Yoshiyahu, "YHWH supports").
sentences.zh: 以赛亚（Yeshayahu，“耶和华拯救”）、耶利米（Yirmeyahu，“耶和华高举”）、撒迦利亚（Zekharyahu，“耶和华记得”）、希西家（Hizkiyahu，“耶和华是我的力量”）和约西亚（Yoshiyahu，“耶和华支持”）等先知和统治者就是这种情况。

sentences.en: Emblematic is the figure of the prophet Elijah, whose Hebrew name Eli-yahu is a synthesis of this encounter, literally meaning «El is YHWH».
sentences.zh: 具有象征意义的是先知以利亚的形象，他的希伯来语名字 Eli-yahu 是这次遭遇的综合，字面意思是“El is YHWH”。

blocks.html_en: The character of YHWH in the archaic texts of the southern tradition is antithetical to that of the transcendent El. YHWH is a concrete, visible, passionate, anthropomorphic god. The text shows him walking in the garden of Eden in the cool of the day (Genesis 3:8), closing the door of Noah's ark with his own hands (Genesis 7:16), or showing Moses his shoulders and back while shielding him in the cleft of the rock (Exodus 33:21-23).

sentences.en: The character of YHWH in the archaic texts of the southern tradition is antithetical to that of the transcendent El.
sentences.zh: 在南方传统的古老文本中，YHWH 的角色与超然的 El 的角色是对立的。

sentences.en: YHWH is a concrete, visible, passionate, anthropomorphic god.
sentences.zh: YHWH 是一位具体的、可见的、热情的、拟人化的神。

sentences.en: The text shows him walking in the garden of Eden in the cool of the day (Genesis 3:8), closing the door of Noah's ark with his own hands (Genesis 7:16), or showing Moses his shoulders and back while shielding him in the cleft of the rock (Exodus 33:21-23).
sentences.zh: 文本显示他在凉爽的日子里行走在伊甸园中（创世记 3:8），亲手关上诺亚方舟的门（创世记 7:16），或者向摩西展示他的肩膀和背部，同时在岩石的缝隙中保护他（出埃及记 33:21-23）。

blocks.html_en: 3. The riddle of Moses

sentences.en: The riddle of Moses
sentences.zh: 摩西之谜

blocks.html_en: The biblical account of the Exodus reflects the historical memory of this encounter between the desert South and Egypt. The very name of Moses is not Hebrew: it derives directly from the Egyptian root mose or msi, simply meaning "born of" or "son" (present in dynastic names such as Thutmose, "son of Thoth", or Ramesses, "son of Ra")8. When Moses flees to Midian after killing an Egyptian overseer beating a Semitic labourer, in the north-western Arabian region identified by Egyptian sources as the cult centre of YHWH, he meets his wife Zipporah. When Zipporah and the other daughters of the priest Reuel/Jethro return home, they describe Moses to their father by saying, explicitly: «An Egyptian delivered us» (Exodus 2:19).

sentences.en: The biblical account of the Exodus reflects the historical memory of this encounter between the desert South and Egypt.
sentences.zh: 圣经对出埃及记的记载反映了南方沙漠和埃及之间这次相遇的历史记忆。

sentences.en: The very name of Moses is not Hebrew: it derives directly from the Egyptian root mose or msi, simply meaning "born of" or "son" (present in dynastic names such as Thutmose, "son of Thoth", or Ramesses, "son of Ra")8.
sentences.zh: 摩西的名字不是希伯来语：它直接源自埃及词根 mose 或 msi，简单的意思是“生于”或“儿子”（出现在诸如图特摩斯（Thutmose）“透特之子”或拉美西斯“拉之子”等王朝名称中）8。

sentences.en: When Moses flees to Midian after killing an Egyptian overseer beating a Semitic labourer, in the north-western Arabian region identified by Egyptian sources as the cult centre of YHWH, he meets his wife Zipporah.
sentences.zh: 当摩西杀死一名殴打一名闪族劳工的埃及监工后，逃往米甸，在埃及消息来源确定的阿拉伯西北部地区，米甸是耶和华的崇拜中心，他遇到了他的妻子西坡拉。

sentences.en: When Zipporah and the other daughters of the priest Reuel/Jethro return home, they describe Moses to their father by saying, explicitly: «An Egyptian delivered us» (Exodus 2:19).
sentences.zh: 当西坡拉和祭司流珥/叶忒罗的其他女儿回家时，她们向父亲描述摩西，明确地说：“有一个埃及人救了我们”（出埃及记 2:19）。

blocks.html_en: To understand the historical context in which such a figure belongs, one must look at the religious upheavals of Egypt's New Kingdom. In the 14th century BCE, Pharaoh Amenhotep IV (Akhenaten) carried out a violent revolution: he erased the traditional Egyptian pantheon, shut the temples and centralised worship on the single sun-god Aten, with the political aim of sidelining the powerful priesthood of Amun at Thebes9. When Akhenaten died, his young son Tutankhaten was forced by the priests of Amun to restore polytheism, changing his own name to Tutankhamun. After the young ruler's death, the army general Horemheb seized power as pharaoh and decreed a damnatio memoriae against Akhenaten, erasing his name from official cartouches and dismantling the capital at Amarna.

sentences.en: To understand the historical context in which such a figure belongs, one must look at the religious upheavals of Egypt's New Kingdom.
sentences.zh: 要了解这样一个人物所属的历史背景，我们必须看看埃及新王国的宗教动乱。

sentences.en: In the 14th century BCE, Pharaoh Amenhotep IV (Akhenaten) carried out a violent revolution: he erased the traditional Egyptian pantheon, shut the temples and centralised worship on the single sun-god Aten, with the political aim of sidelining the powerful priesthood of Amun at Thebes9.
sentences.zh: 公元前14世纪，法老阿蒙霍特普四世（阿肯那吞）发动了一场暴力革命：他废除了传统的埃及万神殿，关闭了寺庙，集中崇拜单一的太阳神阿顿，其政治目的是排挤底比斯强大的阿蒙祭司9。

sentences.en: When Akhenaten died, his young son Tutankhaten was forced by the priests of Amun to restore polytheism, changing his own name to Tutankhamun.
sentences.zh: 阿肯那顿去世后，他的小儿子图坦卡顿在阿蒙祭司的强迫下恢复多神教，并将自己的名字改为图坦卡蒙。

sentences.en: After the young ruler's death, the army general Horemheb seized power as pharaoh and decreed a damnatio memoriae against Akhenaten, erasing his name from official cartouches and dismantling the capital at Amarna.
sentences.zh: 这位年轻的统治者死后，军队将军霍伦赫布以法老的身份夺取了权力，并颁布了针对阿肯那顿的诅咒备忘录，从官方的漩涡花饰上抹去了他的名字，并拆除了阿玛纳的首都。

blocks.html_en: In this climate of religious purges, the thesis of a link between Atenist monotheism and Moses was proposed by Sigmund Freud in his essay Moses and Monotheism (1939). Although Freud's hypothesis of a literally Egyptian, Atenist Moses has remained a minority position among professional Egyptologists, contemporary scholars of cultural memory such as Jan Assmann have explored the trace left in the historical memory of the Near East by the trauma of the Amarna purge108.

sentences.en: In this climate of religious purges, the thesis of a link between Atenist monotheism and Moses was proposed by Sigmund Freud in his essay Moses and Monotheism (1939).
sentences.zh: 在这种宗教清洗的气氛下，西格蒙德·弗洛伊德在他的论文《摩西与一神论》（1939）中提出了阿顿主义一神论和摩西之间的联系。

sentences.en: Although Freud's hypothesis of a literally Egyptian, Atenist Moses has remained a minority position among professional Egyptologists, contemporary scholars of cultural memory such as Jan Assmann have explored the trace left in the historical memory of the Near East by the trauma of the Amarna purge108.
sentences.zh: 尽管弗洛伊德关于阿特尼斯特·摩西（Atenist Moses）确实是埃及人的假设在专业埃及学家中仍然处于少数地位，但扬·阿斯曼（Jan Assmann）等当代文化记忆学者已​​经探索了阿玛纳清洗创伤在近东历史记忆中留下的痕迹108。

blocks.html_en: An element pointing to shared priestly training between Moses, Aaron and the court of the Nile lies in the episode of the sacred wonders performed before the monarch (Exodus 7:11-12)11. When Aaron throws down his staff and turns it into a serpent, or turns water into blood, Pharaoh's magician-priests (the härtummîm) perform exactly the same secret rituals. Moses and Aaron appear to have mastered the same liturgical and theurgic techniques taught in Egyptian priestly schools. The biblical text does not deny the existence of other gods, nor the power of their cults, but rather asserts the supremacy of the god who guides Moses, whose staff-turned-serpent swallows those of the rival deities.

sentences.en: An element pointing to shared priestly training between Moses, Aaron and the court of the Nile lies in the episode of the sacred wonders performed before the monarch (Exodus 7:11-12)11.
sentences.zh: 摩西、亚伦和尼罗河宫廷之间共同进行祭司训练的一个因素在于在君主面前施行神圣奇事的情节（出埃及记 7:11-12）11。

sentences.en: When Aaron throws down his staff and turns it into a serpent, or turns water into blood, Pharaoh's magician-priests (the härtummîm) perform exactly the same secret rituals.
sentences.zh: 当亚伦扔下他的手杖并将其变成蛇或将水变成血时，法老的魔法师祭司（härtummîm）会执行完全相同的秘密仪式。

sentences.en: Moses and Aaron appear to have mastered the same liturgical and theurgic techniques taught in Egyptian priestly schools.
sentences.zh: 摩西和亚伦似乎掌握了埃及祭司学校教授的相同的礼拜仪式和神术技巧。

sentences.en: The biblical text does not deny the existence of other gods, nor the power of their cults, but rather asserts the supremacy of the god who guides Moses, whose staff-turned-serpent swallows those of the rival deities.
sentences.zh: 圣经文本并不否认其他神的存在，也不否认他们的崇拜的力量，而是主张引导摩西的神至高无上，他的杖变成了蛇，吞噬了敌对神的杖。

blocks.html_en: In Exodus 4:10 Moses excuses himself before the divine calling, claiming to be «slow of speech and slow of tongue» (and in Exodus 6:12 he speaks of «uncircumcised lips»)11. Traditional rabbinic interpretation has read this passage as a physical stutter, but some scholars suggest that Moses, raised as an aristocrat at the Nile court, simply did not master the Semitic dialect spoken by the common people.

sentences.en: In Exodus 4:10 Moses excuses himself before the divine calling, claiming to be «slow of speech and slow of tongue» (and in Exodus 6:12 he speaks of «uncircumcised lips»)11.
sentences.zh: 在出埃及记 4 章 10 节中，摩西在神圣的呼召面前为自己辩解，声称自己“言语迟钝，舌头迟钝”（在出埃及记 6 章 12 节中，他谈到“嘴唇未受割礼”）11。

sentences.en: Traditional rabbinic interpretation has read this passage as a physical stutter, but some scholars suggest that Moses, raised as an aristocrat at the Nile court, simply did not master the Semitic dialect spoken by the common people.
sentences.zh: 传统的拉比解释将这段话解读为身体口吃，但一些学者认为，在尼罗河宫廷作为贵族长大的摩西根本不掌握普通百姓所说的闪米特方言。

blocks.html_en: Finally, historical research suggests a measured reading of the alleged mass enslavement. In Exodus 1:11, it is said that the Hebrews were put to work building the store-cities of Pithom (Egyptian Per-Atum) and Rameses (Egyptian Pi-Ramesses)8. Archaeological excavations at Tell el-Dab'a and Qantir have confirmed that these cities in the Nile Delta did exist, and were the site of massive royal building projects under the 19th Dynasty8. However, the Semitic populations present in the Delta, tied to the historical memory of the Hyksos, were in all likelihood resident labourers subject to the royal corvée system12. Had two million slaves fled at once, shattering the Egyptian army, the foreign powers of the era (such as the Hittites or the Canaanite city-states in the Amarna letters) would have widely celebrated and documented Egypt's geopolitical collapse. The silence of neighbouring sources indicates there was no catastrophic collapse, but rather a gradual migration back north of groups of Semitic labourers following a priestly elite breaking with Pharaoh's court12.

sentences.en: Finally, historical research suggests a measured reading of the alleged mass enslavement.
sentences.zh: 最后，历史研究表明对所谓的大规模奴役进行了审慎的解读。

sentences.en: In Exodus 1:11, it is said that the Hebrews were put to work building the store-cities of Pithom (Egyptian Per-Atum) and Rameses (Egyptian Pi-Ramesses)8.
sentences.zh: 在出埃及记 1 章 11 节中，据说希伯来人被派去建造比托姆（埃及 Per-Atum）和拉美西斯（埃及 Pi-Ramesses）8 的储藏城。

sentences.en: Archaeological excavations at Tell el-Dab'a and Qantir have confirmed that these cities in the Nile Delta did exist, and were the site of massive royal building projects under the 19th Dynasty8.
sentences.zh: 特尔达巴 (Tell el-Dab'a) 和坎提尔 (Qantir) 的考古发掘证实，尼罗河三角洲的这些城市确实存在，并且是第十九王朝时期大规模皇家建筑工程的所在地8。

sentences.en: However, the Semitic populations present in the Delta, tied to the historical memory of the Hyksos, were in all likelihood resident labourers subject to the royal corvée system12.
sentences.zh: 然而，与喜克索斯人的历史记忆相关的三角洲地区的闪米特人很可能是受皇家徭役制度管辖的居民劳工12。

sentences.en: Had two million slaves fled at once, shattering the Egyptian army, the foreign powers of the era (such as the Hittites or the Canaanite city-states in the Amarna letters) would have widely celebrated and documented Egypt's geopolitical collapse.
sentences.zh: 如果两百万奴隶立即逃走，粉碎了埃及军队，那么那个时代的外国势力（例如赫梯人或阿玛纳信件中的迦南城邦）就会广泛庆祝并记录埃及地缘政治的崩溃。

sentences.en: The silence of neighbouring sources indicates there was no catastrophic collapse, but rather a gradual migration back north of groups of Semitic labourers following a priestly elite breaking with Pharaoh's court12.
sentences.zh: 邻近消息来源的沉默表明，并没有发生灾难性的崩溃，而是在祭司精英与法老宫廷决裂后，闪米特劳工群体逐渐向北迁移12。

blocks.html_en: 4. The mystery of the bridegroom of blood

sentences.en: The mystery of the bridegroom of blood
sentences.zh: 血新郎之谜

sentences.en: Among the most archaic and unsettling passages in the entire Pentateuch is a very short episode, embedded in Exodus 4:24-2617, which later theology has long tried to soften.

sentences.en: But on the journey back, at a resting place in the desert, something incomprehensible happens:
sentences.zh: 但在返回的途中，在沙漠中的一个休息处，发生了一些令人费解的事情：

sentences.zh: “在途中的一个住宿地点，耶和华遇见了他并想要杀他。

sentences.zh: 西坡拉拿起一块打火石，割下她儿子的包皮，用它碰摩西的脚，说：“你真是我的血新郎！”

sentences.en: So YHWH let him alone.

Only then does God relent and withdraw17.

sentences.en: Zipporah does not hesitate for a second: she grabs a flint stone (not a metal tool, since the oldest ritual tradition of circumcision preserved the use of stone), circumcises her son, and touches Moses's genitals (in the Hebrew euphemism, "feet") with the blood-soaked foreskin, pronouncing the ritual formula Chatan Damim ("bridegroom of blood").
sentences.zh: 西坡拉毫不犹豫：她抓起一块燧石（不是金属工具，因为最古老的割礼传统保留了石头的使用），对她的儿子进行了割礼，并用浸满鲜血的包皮触摸摩西的生殖器（希伯来语委婉语中的“脚”），念出仪式公式Chatan Damim（“血的新郎”）。

blocks.html_en: To explain the episode, biblical criticism turns to the Kenite-Midianite Hypothesis (today among the most credited in scholarly debate, though without unanimous consensus). The biblical text explicitly presents Zipporah as the daughter of Reuel/Jethro, the priest of Midian (Exodus 2:16-21). According to the Kenite-Midianite hypothesis, her family had for generations kept the rites of the desert god at Midian, the original geographic cradle of the cult of YHWH. Moses, having grown up at the Egyptian court, had not been circumcised according to the tribal norm of YHWH. Entering the deity's sacred territory without the mark of the covenant, Moses was regarded by YHWH as a profane outsider to be eliminated. Zipporah, knowing the nature of her father's god, performs an immediate apotropaic act: she uses her son's blood to ritually bind Moses to YHWH, making him a "bridegroom of blood" and saving his life.

sentences.en: To explain the episode, biblical criticism turns to the Kenite-Midianite Hypothesis (today among the most credited in scholarly debate, though without unanimous consensus).
sentences.zh: 为了解释这一事件，圣经批评转向了基尼特-米甸假说（当今学术辩论中最受认可的假说之一，尽管没有达成一致共识）。

sentences.en: The biblical text explicitly presents Zipporah as the daughter of Reuel/Jethro, the priest of Midian (Exodus 2:16-21).
sentences.zh: 圣经明确指出西坡拉是米甸祭司流珥/叶忒罗的女儿（出埃及记 2:16-21）。

sentences.en: According to the Kenite-Midianite hypothesis, her family had for generations kept the rites of the desert god at Midian, the original geographic cradle of the cult of YHWH.
sentences.zh: 根据基尼特-米甸假说，她的家族世世代代在米甸举行沙漠神的仪式，米甸是耶和华崇拜的原始地理摇篮。

sentences.en: Moses, having grown up at the Egyptian court, had not been circumcised according to the tribal norm of YHWH.
sentences.zh: 摩西在埃及宫廷长大，没有按照耶和华的部落规范受过割礼。

sentences.en: Entering the deity's sacred territory without the mark of the covenant, Moses was regarded by YHWH as a profane outsider to be eliminated.
sentences.zh: 摩西在没有圣约标记的情况下进入神的神圣领地，被耶和华视为亵渎的外来者并予以消灭。

sentences.en: Zipporah, knowing the nature of her father's god, performs an immediate apotropaic act: she uses her son's blood to ritually bind Moses to YHWH, making him a "bridegroom of blood" and saving his life.
sentences.zh: 西坡拉知道了她父亲神的本质，立即做出了驱邪行为：她用儿子的血在仪式上将摩西与耶和华结合在一起，使他成为“血的新郎”并拯救了他的生命。

blocks.html_en: The Midianite origin and the originally archaic, non-monotheistic character of this cult also emerge clearly from the later encounter between the Israelites and Jethro in the desert (Exodus 18:11), where the Midianite priest exclaims: «Now I know that YHWH is greater than all gods» (mi-kol ha-elohim). In a purely monotheistic context, this statement would make no sense, since one does not call a deity the greatest if the others do not exist. It is the testimony of a monolatrous, henotheistic phase, confirmed by the First Commandment itself (Exodus 20:3: «You shall have no other gods before me»), which forbids the worship of other deities without denying their ontological existence2.

sentences.en: The Midianite origin and the originally archaic, non-monotheistic character of this cult also emerge clearly from the later encounter between the Israelites and Jethro in the desert (Exodus 18:11), where the Midianite priest exclaims: «Now I know that YHWH is greater than all gods» (mi-kol ha-elohim).
sentences.zh: 米甸的起源和这种崇拜最初古老的、非一神论的特征也从后来以色列人和叶忒罗在沙漠中的相遇中清楚地显现出来（出埃及记 18:11），米甸祭司惊呼道：“现在我知道耶和华比所有的神都伟大”（mi-kol ha-elohim）。

sentences.en: In a purely monotheistic context, this statement would make no sense, since one does not call a deity the greatest if the others do not exist.
sentences.zh: 在纯粹的一神论背景下，这种说法是没有意义的，因为如果其他神不存在，人们就不会称神为最伟大的。

sentences.en: It is the testimony of a monolatrous, henotheistic phase, confirmed by the First Commandment itself (Exodus 20:3: «You shall have no other gods before me»), which forbids the worship of other deities without denying their ontological existence2.
sentences.zh: 这是单一崇拜、单一神论阶段的见证，第一条诫命本身也证实了这一点（出埃及记 20:3：“除了我以外，你不可有别的神”），它禁止崇拜其他神祇，但又不否认其本体论的存在2。

blocks.html_en: A detail some scholars read as a further clue, though hardly conclusive, follows immediately after, in Exodus 18:12: during the sacrifice that seals the encounter, it is neither Moses nor Aaron who officiates the rite, but Jethro himself, who brings the burnt offering and sacrifices to God, while Aaron and all the elders of Israel simply join the ritual meal "before God" together with Moses's father-in-law. That a Midianite priest presides over the ceremony, rather than the two Hebrew leaders fresh out of Egypt, has sometimes been read as a possible sign that Jethro was not merely joining someone else's cult, but already held a recognised priestly role toward YHWH; this remains an inference, though, not a settled fact.

sentences.zh: 主持仪式的是一位米甸祭司，而不是两位刚从埃及出来的希伯来领袖，有时被解读为一个可能的迹象，表明叶忒罗不仅加入了别人的邪教，而且已经在耶和华面前担任了公认的祭司角色；但这仍然是一个推论，并不是一个确定的事实。

blocks.html_en: 5. The Levites: the birth of a priestly caste

sentences.en: The Levites: the birth of a priestly caste
sentences.zh: 利未人：祭司阶层的诞生

blocks.html_en: The Egyptian legacy and ideological fanaticism converged into a single tribe: the Levites. Among the twelve tribes of Israel, the priestly tribe of the Levites is the only one to preserve several names of credited Egyptian etymology, such as Moses (from Egyptian Msi, "born of"), Phinehas (from Egyptian Pa-nehesi, "the Nubian"), Hophni (from Egyptian Hfnw, "tadpole") and Pashhur (from Egyptian p3 sri n ḥr or pss-ḥr, "son of Horus" or "portion of Horus").

sentences.en: The Egyptian legacy and ideological fanaticism converged into a single tribe: the Levites.
sentences.zh: 埃及的遗产和意识形态的狂热汇聚成一个部落：利未人。

sentences.en: Among the twelve tribes of Israel, the priestly tribe of the Levites is the only one to preserve several names of credited Egyptian etymology, such as Moses (from Egyptian Msi, "born of"), Phinehas (from Egyptian Pa-nehesi, "the Nubian"), Hophni (from Egyptian Hfnw, "tadpole") and Pashhur (from Egyptian p3 sri n ḥr or pss-ḥr, "son of Horus" or "portion of Horus").
sentences.zh: 在以色列的十二个部落中，利未人的祭司部落是唯一保留了几个埃及词源名称的部落，例如摩西（来自埃及语 Msi，“出生于”）、非尼哈斯（来自埃及语 Pa-nehesi，“努比亚人”）、霍弗尼（来自埃及语 Hfnw，“蝌蚪”）和帕什胡尔（来自埃及语 p3 sri n ḥr 或 pss-ḥr，“之子”）荷鲁斯”或“荷鲁斯的一部分”）。

blocks.html_en: The key episode of rigid priestly fanaticism takes place during the march through the desert: the story of the Golden Calf (Exodus 32)13. Faced with the masses' return to the syncretic cults they had betrayed, Moses gathers the Levites and orders a systematic slaughter: three thousand men (including brothers, friends and neighbours) are massacred by the priests to impose, with blood, the exclusive monotheistic cult of YHWH (Exodus 32:26-28).

sentences.en: The key episode of rigid priestly fanaticism takes place during the march through the desert: the story of the Golden Calf (Exodus 32)13.
sentences.zh: 严格的祭司狂热的关键情节发生在穿越沙漠的过程中：金牛犊的故事（出埃及记 32）13。

sentences.en: Faced with the masses' return to the syncretic cults they had betrayed, Moses gathers the Levites and orders a systematic slaughter: three thousand men (including brothers, friends and neighbours) are massacred by the priests to impose, with blood, the exclusive monotheistic cult of YHWH (Exodus 32:26-28).
sentences.zh: 面对大众回归他们所背叛的融合崇拜，摩西聚集了利未人，下令进行系统性的屠杀：祭司们屠杀了三千人（包括兄弟、朋友和邻居），以血腥的方式强加对耶和华的唯一一神崇拜（出埃及记 32:26-28）。

blocks.html_en: Beyond the ideological violence, the Levites brought into the desert a sophisticated ritual culture unknown to the nomads of Sinai, modelled almost entirely on the liturgy of the Nile temples14. Levitical priests were required to wear only pure linen garments (shesh, from the Egyptian term šs), with wool strictly forbidden (Leviticus 6:3)14. This is a telling prescription: wool was the natural fibre produced daily by the desert's nomadic populations through sheep and goat herding, while linen required sowing, cultivation and irrigation on fertile farmland, a resource typical of the Nile valley and entirely impossible to produce in the desert. Mandating linen and excluding wool means the priestly norm did not originate among the Bedouin of Sinai, but was imported directly from the prescriptive sacred dress of the Egyptian priestly caste. Likewise, the daily purification rituals with water, the full-body shaving required of the Levites (Numbers 8:7) and the prohibition on contact with corpses mirror the rules of the Karnak sanctuaries. Finally, the structure of the Tabernacle and the proportions of the Ark of the Covenant are identical to the military encampment of Ramesses II at the Battle of Kadesh and to the gilded wooden shrines found in Tutankhamun's tomb15. Taken individually, these elements do not amount to proof. Taken together, they have been interpreted by some scholars as evidence of a significant Egyptian influence on the formation of the Levitical tradition.

sentences.en: Beyond the ideological violence, the Levites brought into the desert a sophisticated ritual culture unknown to the nomads of Sinai, modelled almost entirely on the liturgy of the Nile temples14.
sentences.zh: 除了意识形态的暴力之外，利未人还给沙漠带来了西奈游牧民族所不知道的复杂的仪式文化，这种文化几乎完全模仿尼罗河神庙的礼拜仪式14。

sentences.en: Levitical priests were required to wear only pure linen garments (shesh, from the Egyptian term šs), with wool strictly forbidden (Leviticus 6:3)14.
sentences.zh: 利未祭司必须只穿纯亚麻衣服（shesh，来自埃及术语 šs），严禁穿羊毛衣服（利未记 6:3）14。

sentences.en: Mandating linen and excluding wool means the priestly norm did not originate among the Bedouin of Sinai, but was imported directly from the prescriptive sacred dress of the Egyptian priestly caste.
sentences.zh: 规定使用亚麻布而排除羊毛意味着祭司规范并非起源于西奈的贝都因人，而是直接从埃及祭司种姓规定的神圣服装中引进的。

sentences.en: Likewise, the daily purification rituals with water, the full-body shaving required of the Levites (Numbers 8:7) and the prohibition on contact with corpses mirror the rules of the Karnak sanctuaries.
sentences.zh: 同样，每天的用水净化仪式、利未人要求的全身剃毛（民数记 8:7）以及禁止接触尸体都反映了卡纳克神庙的规则。

sentences.en: Finally, the structure of the Tabernacle and the proportions of the Ark of the Covenant are identical to the military encampment of Ramesses II at the Battle of Kadesh and to the gilded wooden shrines found in Tutankhamun's tomb15.
sentences.zh: 最后，会幕的结构和约柜的比例与卡迭石战役中拉美西斯二世的军营以及图坦卡蒙墓中发现的镀金木制神龛相同15。

sentences.zh: 单独来看，这些要素并不能构成证据。

sentences.en: Taken together, they have been interpreted by some scholars as evidence of a significant Egyptian influence on the formation of the Levitical tradition.
